title: In New Zealand’s 2008 election, 4.07% of party votes won no seats, but 3.65% won five
body: On 26 October 2026 advance voting opened for New Zealand’s general election of 7 November, Reuters [reported](https://www.thestar.com.my/news/world/2026/10/26/voting-opens-in-new-zealand-for-november-7-election-with-no-clear-frontrunner). New Zealand uses mixed-member proportional voting (MMP): each voter has an electorate vote, which elects a local MP in each of 71 electorates, and a party vote, which decides how many of the 120 seats each party gets, in proportion. A party’s local winners count inside its share, and MPs from its list fill the rest. But a party shares in the seats only with 5% of the party vote or at least one electorate, as this [guide to the system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_system_of_New_Zealand) explains. In 2008 New Zealand First won 4.07% of the party vote and no electorate, so its 95,356 votes elected no one; ACT won 3.65%, but its leader Rodney Hide held Epsom, so ACT got 5 seats, 4 of them from its list. A party that wins more electorates than its share keeps them as overhang seats: in 2008 the Māori Party won 5 electorates on a party vote worth 3 seats, and parliament had 122 members.

slides.question: New Zealand’s parliament normally has 120 seats. How many MPs did its 2008 general election produce?
slides.explanation: 122: the Māori Party won 5 electorates while its party vote was worth only 3 seats, and kept the 2 extra as overhang seats.

slides.alt: Animation on night-ocean blue: a ballot with a party vote and an electorate vote; 71 electorates; 120 seats shared in proportion, an example party's 36 as 20 local and 16 list; the 5% or one-electorate gate; 2008 bars for New Zealand First and ACT; a hemicycle growing to 122 seats.

slides.prompt: Switch on both what-ifs: ACT loses Epsom and New Zealand First wins a seat. What are their 2008 votes worth then?
slides.takeaway: Without Epsom, ACT’s 3.65% wins nothing; with one electorate, New Zealand First’s 4.07% would have been worth 5 seats. One local seat decides whether a small party’s votes count.

slides.heading: How New Zealand’s two votes become seats

steps.label: A party vote and an electorate vote
In: 5% of party votes, or one electorate
Party votes share out the 120 seats
Local winners count inside each share

slides.heading: Seats won in 2008, with each party’s share of the party vote
slides.note: ACT held the Epsom electorate; the Māori Party won 5 electorates; the Greens passed 5%.

slides.question: Under New Zealand’s MMP, what decides how many seats in all a party gets, once it qualifies?
options: Its share of the party vote
slides.explanation: The party vote. Local winners count inside that share; only a party that wins more electorates than its share gets extra, overhang seats.
